UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                                Docket No. ER26-3380-000


               COMMENTS OF THE INSTITUTE FOR POLICY INTEGRITY
                  AT NEW YORK UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF LAW ON
                PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C. SECTION 205 FILING
              TO IMPLEMENT RELIABILITY BACKSTOP PROCUREMENT


        The Institute for Policy Integrity at New York University School of Law (Policy

Integrity)1 respectfully submits the following comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission (FERC) regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM)’s Federal Power Act (FPA)

Section 205 proposed tariff implementing Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP). Policy

Integrity is a non-partisan think tank dedicated to improving the quality of government

decisionmaking through advocacy and scholarship in the fields of administrative law, economics,

and public policy.

        On July 31, 2026, pursuant to Section 205 of the FPA, PJM filed for revisions to its Open

Access Transmission Tariff to implement RBP, which will include a Reliability Backstop

Auction (Backstop Auction). These revisions are designed to address the capacity shortfall in the

2028/2029 Base Residual Auction (BRA, or Legacy Capacity Market) and future BRA shortfalls

that PJM anticipates will occur.2 Part I of these comments provides context for PJM’s proposed

tariff revisions. Part II explains that FERC should reject PJM’s proposed tariff because PJM has



1
 This document does not purport to present the views, if any, of New York University School of Law.
2
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns
Stemming from Large Loads, 7-8, 27-28 (filed July 31, 2026) (hereinafter, Tariff Filing).


                                                                                                       1
 failed, for multiple reasons, to meet its burden to show that the Backstop Auction is just and

reasonable. These reasons include:

         1) PJM cannot sufficiently determine whether long-term, systemic problems exist in the

             capacity market before three consecutive BRA shortfalls occur;

         2) The Backstop Auction will not isolate the Legacy Capacity Market from the costs of

             large load growth;

         3) PJM can address its resource adequacy problems at lower cost and with less risk of

             cost-shifting through other means.

         Part III asserts, in the alternative, that FERC should find that PJM can demonstrate its

proposed tariff is just and reasonable only if PJM amends the design of the Backstop Auction to

mitigate the likelihood that it will result in unjust and unreasonable rates.3 Part III sets out tariff

amendments that PJM can adopt to reduce the risk that its tariff will result in unjust and

unreasonable rates.

    I.   BACKGROUND

         On December 17, 2025, PJM announced that the 2027/2028 BRA cleared 6,623 MW

short of its procurement target.4 In a report investigating the causes of this shortfall, PJM

Generation Resources, PJM INSIDE LINES (Dec. 17, 2025), https://perma.cc/2P3E-4Z75. PJM’s procurement target
for the BRA is based on load forecasts submitted by Electric Distribution Companies (EDCs) for each zone. PJM

directed PJM Staff to implement a host of reforms to the load forecasting process, including state review of large
load additions, addressing duplicative requests, and the use of additional third-party review and increased

 predicted that capacity market shortfalls would likely continue over the next decade, driven by

forecasted demand growth from data centers and other customers.5 PJM’s report also found that

the administrative price collar imposed on the capacity market likely exacerbated the deficit.6

        On January 15, 2026, the White House Natural Energy Dominance Council and the PJM

Governors’ Coalition signed a “Statement of Principles Regarding PJM” (Statement of

Principles), which directed PJM to “[p]rovide 15-year price certainty for new capacity

resources.”7 The Statement of Principles suggested PJM could provide price certainty by

“holding a Reliability Backstop Auction to procure new capacity resources commencing no later

than September 2026.”8 In response, the PJM Board initiated a Critical Issue Fast Path (CIFP)

process to develop an RBP proposal and PJM subsequently convened a series of stakeholder

meetings to solicit feedback.9 In the same CIFP, PJM also solicited stakeholder feedback on

Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS), formerly denoted “Connect and Manage,” a

program that would require new large loads to bring their own new capacity to the grid, or be

subject to interruptible service under certain emergency conditions.10 On July 14, 2026, in the

midst of the RBP stakeholder process, PJM announced that the 2028/2029 BRA cleared short of

its procurement target by 6,831 MW.11

          PJM’s final RBP proposal comprises two elements to occur in parallel, only one of which

requires FERC approval. First, PJM will facilitate matching between customers and suppliers

who want to enter bilateral capacity contracts. PJM’s consultant issued a Request for Proposals

on June 9, 2026, and the matching process will occur over the course of six to nine months,

expected to start in late August.12 PJM need not amend the tariff for this private contracting

process because PJM will merely facilitate voluntary negotiations and not participate as a party.

Second, PJM proposes to run a Backstop Auction, starting on September 30, 2026, to procure

enough capacity to cover the 2028/2029 BRA shortfall.13 That Backstop Auction would be

subject to the following proposed rules:

     ● The Backstop Auction would accept supply bids only from “new”14 capacity resources,

         which can have an in-service date any time after the 2028/2029 DY and before June

         2032;

     ● The Backstop Auction would secure capacity for 15-year terms. If a supplier bids

         capacity that will begin service later than 2028/2029 DY, the contract term would extend

         to the remainder of the 15-year term (e.g., a generator coming online in 2032 would only

         have a ten-year contract);




12
   Tariff Filing, supra n. 2, 30-31; PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., CIFP Reliability Backstop Procurement - PJM
Board Decision, 1 (July 31, 2026), https://perma.cc/EA2Q-X5JD (hereinafter, RBP Board Decision); Charles River
Associates, PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement Bilateral Request for Proposal (June 9, 2026),
https://perma.cc/BN29-2UAF.
13
   PJM will target September 30, 2026 to begin bid solicitation, which would close three weeks later (October 21,
2026). The subsequent clearing and selection process would conclude six weeks after the offer submission window
closes, and the sellers would be notified as soon as practicable once the backstop auction ends. Tariff Filing, supra
n. 2, 27, 48. The initial target for the backstop auction is approximately 6.8 GW, which PJM will reduce based on
evidence of bilateral contracts for new capacity. See infra fn. 16.
14
   PJM defines “new” capacity to determine which supply qualifies to bid into the backstop auction more narrowly
than PJM defines “new” capacity to determine what qualifies to decrement the procurement target. Tariff Filing,
supra n. 2, 36, 51.


                                                                                                                        4
      ● Each Backstop Auction contract would work as a “contract for differences” against future

         capacity auction prices with PJM as the counterparty;15

     ● The procurement target would be set as the amount of the 2028/29 BRA shortfall, less

         any capacity secured in bilateral contracts prior to the Backstop Auction or subject to

         state peak shaving laws;16

     ● The auction mechanism would be “pay-as-bid”17 with a price cap set at $555/MW-day

         UCAP (1.5 x Net Cost of New Entry) for the volume-weighted average of the levelized

         cost of all selected offers;18

     ● PJM would allocate Backstop Auction costs to zones based on each zone’s pro rata share

         of the total costs. PJM would then allocate costs within zones to Load Serving Entities

         (LSEs) based on cost allocation methodologies submitted by the state or Relevant

         Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (RERRA);

     ● If states or RERRAs do not provide PJM with a cost allocation methodology, PJM would
         revert to using Peak Load Contribution to allocate Backstop Auction costs among

         LSEs.19


15
   E.g. For any capacity contracted in the RBP for 2030, suppliers will bid that capacity into the 2030 BRA at $0,
and either suppliers or Load Serving Entities (LSEs) will pay the difference between the RBP price and the BRA
price, depending on which is higher. So, for example, if the BRA clears at $100/MW-day, but PJM accepts a
supplier’s bid for capacity at $200/MW-day in the backstop auction, that supplier would receive $100/MW-day in
the BRA, and PJM would compensate that supplier with an additional $100/MW-day, so the supplier receives a total
of $200/MW-day. Conversely, if the BRA clears at $200/MW-day, and the backstop auction clears at $100/MW-
day, the suppliers would have to pay back $100/MW-day to the LSEs and would effectively receive a total of
$100/MW-day.
16
   The window for suppliers to submit bids will run three weeks after the auction opening date (PJM proposes that
this will start on September 30, 2026, but acknowledges that there may be delays). If the auction opens on
September 30, as proposed, the window for bid solicitation will close on October 21, 2026. At any time during this
window, LSEs can submit evidence of bilateral contracts and PJM will subtract these contracts from the
procurement target.
17
   Under a pay-as-bid system, suppliers are paid the amount of the bid they offer, as opposed to the clearing price.
18
   For example, a supplier could bid in an offer over $555/MW-day and its bid may still be accepted if enough other
suppliers bid in below the price cap, such that the overall average of all bids remains below $555/MW-day.
19
   Tariff Filing, supra n. 2, 97-99. There are limited opt-out provisions for (1) zones that can demonstrate an
inability to allocate costs to large loads; and (2) states that demonstrate they have peak-shaving programs codified in

  II.     FERC should reject the proposed tariff revisions because PJM has failed to
         demonstrate that the Backstop Auction is just and reasonable.

         PJM has not met its burden to demonstrate that the Backstop Auction is just and

reasonable for the following reasons:

             1) PJM has not adequately explained why it is appropriate to run the Backstop

                  Auction before three consecutive BRA shortfalls indicate long-term, systemic

                  market problems;

             2) PJM has not adequately explained why the Backstop Auction is appropriate given

                  that it will not isolate the capacity market from the impacts of large load growth;

                  and

             3) PJM has not adequately explained why the Backstop Auction is warranted given

                  that other alternatives will address the same problems at lower cost and with less

                  risk of cost-shifting.

         Because PJM cannot demonstrate that its proposed tariff is within the zone of

reasonableness and has not provided substantial evidence showing that the revisions will result in

just and reasonable rates, FERC should reject the proposed tariff revisions.20

             A. PJM must prove that its proposed tariff revisions are just and reasonable
                and supported by substantial evidence.

         Under FPA section 205, a party seeking to revise its tariff bears the burden of proof to

demonstrate that its revisions will result in “just and reasonable” rates.21 The just and reasonable




state law. Id. at 44-45. PJM indicates that the first category is “designed to address a limited regulatory gap faced by
cooperatives and municipal utilities whose rates are not regulated by the states.” Id.
20
   16 U.S.C. § 824d(e); New York Pub. Serv. Comm’n v. FERC, 104 F.4th 886, 890 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (NYPSC v.
FERC).
21
   See id.


                                                                                                                       6
 standard requires “a balancing of investor and consumer interests.”22 Rates must be high enough

to allow utilities to recover their costs and maintain financial integrity, but they must be low

enough to avoid imposing excessive costs on consumers.23 Rates may also be unjust and

unreasonable if they fail to ensure reliable service, or do not assign costs to customers “roughly

commensurate” according to who benefits from such costs.24 FERC must find that a rate

proponent has provided “substantial evidence” that its filing is just and reasonable before FERC

can approve the revised tariff.25 This inquiry is equivalent to “arbitrary and capricious” review

under the Administrative Procedure Act.26

         PJM filed its revised tariff pursuant to section 205, which requires PJM to prove that its

proposed revisions are just and reasonable, i.e., that its rates will not excessively burden

consumers, unfairly allocate costs, or lead to reliability problems. If FERC finds that PJM has

not provided substantial evidence supporting its assertion that the proposed tariff revisions are

just and reasonable, FERC must reject the filing.27




22
   Federal Power Comm’n v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591, 603 (1944) (finding that the just and reasonable
standard requires a balancing of investor and consumer interests); Jersey Cent. Power & Light v. FERC, 810 F.2d
1168, 1172 (D.C. Cir. 1987) (applying the Hope holding to electric rates).
23
   Id.; NYPSC v. FERC, 104 F.4th at 890 (“[T]here is not a single ‘just and reasonable rate’ but rather a “zone of

rates.”).
24
   Advanced Energy Mgmt. All. v. FERC, 860 F.3d 656, 661 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (finding that failure to provide reliable
service is relevant to the just and reasonable standard); Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1255
(D.C. Cir. 2018) (Old Dominion) (establishing the cost causation principle); Ill. Commerce Comm’n v. FERC, 576
F.3d 470, 477 (7th Cir. 2009) (finding that the cost causation principle requires benefits to be “roughly
commensurate” with costs) (ICC v. FERC).
25
   16 U.S.C. § 824l(b); New Jersey Bd. of Public Utils. v. FERC, 744 F.3d 74, 93 (3rd Cir. 2014) (finding that the
substantial evidence standard requires “more than a scintilla, but . . . less than a preponderance of the evidence.”)
(NJBPU v. FERC).
26

standard is equivalent to “arbitrary and capricious” review under the Administrative Procedure Act); Ass’n of Data
Processing Service Orgs. v. Bd. of Governors of the Fed. Reserve Sys., 745 F.2d 677, 681-86 (D.C. Cir. 1984).

              B. FERC should reject the proposed tariff because PJM has not adequately
                explained why it is appropriate to run the Backstop Auction before three
                consecutive BRA shortfalls indicate long-term, systemic market problems.

        PJM’s current tariff authorizes PJM to hold a reliability backstop auction when three

consecutive BRAs clear short of the procurement target.28 It is important that PJM can run a

backstop auction only when there are long-term systemic issues in the BRA, not based on short-

term market dynamics, because consistent and stable market rules are critical for investment.

FERC should reject the revised tariff because PJM has not provided substantial evidence to

justify its decision to depart from the backstop provisions in its existing tariff, particularly given

rapid and substantial reform occurring at the state and federal levels.29

        Although the BRA cleared short of its target two years in a row, these shortfalls do not

provide sufficient evidence that revising PJM’s current tariff is warranted. First, it is unclear

whether the two BRA shortfalls would count towards triggering a backstop auction. The current

tariff triggers a backstop auction only after three consecutive BRA shortfalls.30 But the tariff

contemplates that BRAs will acquire capacity three years in advance of the targeted delivery

year. PJM has strayed from the auction schedule stipulated in the tariff and held the last two

auctions to acquire capacity for delivery years closely proximate to the auction year.31 Because

of these delays, PJM has demonstrated evidence for only two near-term years of capacity

shortfalls.32 PJM has not adequately explained why two years of near-term predicted capacity

shortfalls are sufficient to identify systemic problems in the BRA, when the current tariff

 requires PJM to establish a showing of long-term resource adequacy issues (i.e., shortfalls

expected in three, four, and five years in the future) before authorizing a backstop auction.

        Second, PJM has not adequately explained why tariff revisions are appropriate

considering recent efforts to encourage more investment in capacity resources and to accelerate

resource interconnections. PJM and its member states initiated a slew of reforms after the

2027/2028 BRA shortfall specifically designed to bring more supply online. These reforms need

time to work. PJM recently implemented comprehensive interconnection reform to clear its

queue backlog and substantially reduce waiting times.33 The window for the first group of

applicants under PJM’s new “first ready, first served” interconnection process concluded in April

2026 with over 800 projects representing 220 GW of capacity.34 PJM recently filed tariff

revisions to reform its interconnection process even further to comply with Order 2023.35 These

reforms are pending before the Commission and PJM will likely implement them soon.36 FERC

also recently approved PJM’s proposal for an Expedited Interconnection Track, a temporary

process to quickly advance large projects that address urgent capacity needs.37 This new program

took effect July 31, 2026, so PJM would not be able to judge its effectiveness before running the

Backstop Auction.

        PJM member states are also acting to attract investment in capacity. Virginia passed a

law in April 2026 that comprehensively reformed the solar siting process, creating a uniform

 statewide process that exempts larger solar projects from certain local regulations.38 Virginia also

created a task force to advance energy affordability and distributed energy, and passed a law

increasing battery storage targets for state utilities.39 In New Jersey, Governor Mikie Sherrill

signed legislation to launch a new procurement process for nuclear generation.40 In

impact PJM’s demand growth projections.41

        PJM has not explained how or why the proposed tariff revisions are appropriate given

these recent developments, including its own efforts to get new resources online more quickly.

PJM has not adequately explained why it is appropriate to lock in new capacity contracts for 15-

year terms when state and regional reforms will likely result in more abundant supply for future

BRAs. Accordingly, FERC should not approve the tariff revisions because PJM has not

adequately explained or provided substantial evidence that its departure from the terms of the

current tariff is just and reasonable.

             C. The Backstop Auction will not isolate the Legacy Capacity Market from the
                impacts of large load growth.

        PJM has not adequately justified its decision to run the Backstop Auction given that the

Backstop Auction will not shield the Legacy Capacity Market from the rate impacts of large load

growth. Running a backstop auction, regardless of how PJM designs it, will inevitably impact the

 Legacy Capacity Market. As proposed, the Backstop Auction and the Legacy Capacity Market

are tied together by a contract-for-differences structure. Each supplier who clears a bid in the

Backstop Auction would also have to bid its committed capacity into the Legacy Capacity

Market at $0.42 Suppliers would then receive the BRA clearing price, either topped up or

subtracted, to match the price they received in the Backstop Auction.43 Under this structure, the

results of the Backstop Auction would inevitably affect prices in the Legacy Capacity Market.

And these effects would persist for the next 15 years because capacity committed through the

Backstop Auction must also bid into the BRA for each year of its contract. Even if PJM did not

opt to run the Backstop Auction as a contract-for-differences, any version of a backstop auction

would still affect the Legacy Capacity Market. PJM would still have to account for capacity

committed through a backstop auction by adjusting the BRA procurement target.44

         The exact relationship between the Backstop Auction and the Legacy Capacity Market

would change depending on how accurately PJM sets the procurement target for the Backstop

Auction. PJM sets the procurement target for the Legacy Capacity Market based on load

forecasts submitted by Electric Distribution Companies (EDCs), and PJM proposes to set the

procurement target for the Backstop Auction as the amount of shortfall in the 2028/2029 BRA,

approximately 6.8 GW.45 If PJM has set the target too high and procures more capacity in the

Backstop Auction than is actually necessary to serve data centers, the offer requirement for new

backstop resources will depress clearing prices in the Legacy Capacity Market. The BRA

clearing price would fall because capacity committed through the Backstop Auction would flood

prices in the Legacy Capacity Market enough, prices may not be high enough to compensate

existing suppliers, and they may retire, leading to resource adequacy problems. If enough

generators retire, it could force PJM to rely on expensive emergency procedures, such as

Reliability Must Run (RMR) agreements or requesting the Department of Energy (DOE) to issue

emergency orders under FPA section 202(c).46 Even if the market eventually responds to these

retirements with price increases, PJM would still be forced to rely in the short-term on costly,

and inefficient reliability fixes may impose excessive burden on consumers, which could result

in unjust and unreasonable rates.

        If PJM has set the procurement target too low, and procures less capacity than data

centers need, it could lead to similar outcomes. In a tight market for supply, there may not be

enough capacity to meet the procurement target for both the Backstop Auction and the Legacy

Capacity Market. A tight supply market is not an unlikely scenario, since supply is scarce in

PJM, due to a variety of problems including supply chain shortages and interconnection queue

delays.47 When there is not enough supply to go around, suppliers will be more likely to offer

their resources into the Backstop Auction, which has a higher price cap than the upcoming

2029/2030 BRA.48 The Backstop Auction may also be appealing to resources that are further

 advanced in the interconnection queue, such as projects approved under the Reliability Resource

Initiative (RRI), because the Backstop Auction offers price certainty for 15 years, whereas the

Legacy Capacity Market offers one-year contracts.49

        If enough suppliers opt for the Backstop Auction instead of the Legacy Capacity Market,

the Legacy Capacity Market may not be able to maintain resource adequacy as large loads come

online. Thus, the Backstop Auction would not insulate non-large load ratepayers from the

impacts of large load growth. If PJM implements IRAS, more new large load growth than

expected will not cause problems for the Legacy Capacity Market, since the new large loads

the zonal level. If large load growth is expected in the Mid-Atlantic zone, but it actually

materializes in the Western Region, LSEs in the Mid-Atlantic zone would still have to bear those

costs. This cost allocation problem sits squarely within PJM’s jurisdiction because incorrectly

assigning capacity costs at the zonal level affects wholesale customers, not just retail

customers.92

        To mitigate this cost-shifting problem, PJM should allow LSEs to trade capacity credits

with each other across different zones to serve load growth as needed. This provision was part of

             C. FERC should require PJM to adjust the Backstop Auction design to avoid
                overpaying for capacity.

        FERC should instruct PJM that it cannot demonstrate its proposed market design is just

and reasonable unless PJM adopts measures to mitigate the risk that the Backstop Auction will

impose excessive burden on consumers. To do this, FERC should require PJM to eliminate the

requirement that demand response resources must have a 15-year agreement in place to

participate in the Backstop Auction.94 Demand response resources are some of the least

expensive capacity resources available and imposing onerous restrictions on their participation

will artificially increase costs.95 PJM allows other resources to place bids for capacity service

beginning in 2032, so requiring demand response suppliers to commit starting in 2028/2029 DY

is unduly discriminatory.96

IV.     Conclusion

        FERC should reject PJM’s proposed tariff revisions because the Backstop Auction is not

just and reasonable. In the alternative, if FERC is inclined to permit PJM to implement some

version of the Backstop Auction, FERC should require PJM to refile its proposed tariff with
